lesson.menu_desc: The language of a career that changed direction -- used to, be used to and getting used to
lesson.subtitle: Lesson 7 -- What You Used to Do
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Amanda Merlini | Lesson 7 -- What You Used to Do
lesson.grammar_point: used to, be used to and get used to

vocab.title: Match each expression to its meaning
defs: to stop doing something slowly, over a period, instead of all at once
the areas of law a person actually works in
to pass a matter, with everything it needs, to the person who continues it
back then, when the situation was different from now
a change of direction inside a professional life
before now, in an earlier stage of the story
to accept a new responsibility and add it to what you already have
a period when a lot has to be learned very fast

items.situation: Somebody asks what your work looked like three years ago.
tips: I used to spend most of my week on supply contracts.
used to + infinitive, for a habit that is over.

items.situation: They ask whether that is still true.
tips: Not any more. Now I work on environmental and regulatory matters.
The contrast is the point: used to for then, present simple for now.

items.situation: They ask: "Did you use to work with land law?"
tips: No, I did not use to work with land law at all, and now it is half my week.
In the question and the negative, use to loses the d.

items.situation: They ask whether the new area feels strange.
tips: Less every week. I am getting used to reading technical annexes.
get used to + ing, for the process of adapting.

items.situation: A colleague asks how you cope with the volume of new documents.
tips: I am used to long contracts, so the length is not the hard part. The science is.
be used to + noun or ing, for something already familiar.

items.situation: Your manager asks what you are giving up to take this on.
tips: I am phasing out the routine supply contracts and handing them over to the team.
Two phrasal verbs, one sentence, and a clear answer.

listenings.text: Amanda, it is Karin. Quick one, and it is a good problem. The board approved the project on Tuesday, which means the environmental work stops being a side file and becomes part of your job description. So we have to decide what leaves your desk. My suggestion is this. The routine supply contracts, the ones that used to take two days a week, go to the team, with a template and a short note from you. The disputes stay with you, because nobody else has the history. And the new file grows. I know this is a steep learning curve, and I know you did not use to work with land law at all. That is also why the board wanted you and not an outside firm. Think about it and tell me on Thursday what you want to hand over and what you want to keep.

People ask me what it was like to change area after twelve years, and the honest answer has three parts. The first year was humiliating, and I mean that as a technical description, not as a complaint. I used to be the person in the room who knew the answer, and suddenly I was the person asking what a word meant. The second part is that the old knowledge does not disappear, it changes function. I do not draft the same contracts any more, but I read every new one with twelve years of disputes behind my eyes, and that is worth more here than it was where I learned it. And the third part is the one nobody tells you. You never stop feeling new, you just get used to feeling new. When that stops being uncomfortable, the move is finished.

extra_audio.text: Start with what your work used to be, before the change. Then say what happened, and when. Then say what your work is now. Then say what you are still getting used to. And finally, say what you are keeping from the old work, and why it still matters.
